sections.heading: Parallelism in lists
body: Give list items the same kind of wording: hiking, swimming, and biking; or to run, to jump, and to swim.
Compare the underlined item with the unchanged items. Keep an -ing pattern or a to + verb pattern, called an infinitive. Do not switch between them when the list needs matching forms.
A shared to can govern several verbs: to run, jump, and swim. Repeating to is also valid. Do not reject an option solely because it omits an optional repeated word.
The same principle applies to finite verbs and relative clauses; a shared who can govern coordinated predicates.

examples.text: On weekends Theo enjoys hiking, swimming, and biking.
examples.label: All three items are -ing forms

examples.text: On weekends Theo enjoys hiking, swimming, and to bike.
examples.label: Third item switches to an infinitive

examples.text: The guide checks the route, monitors the weather, and adjusts the schedule.
examples.label: All three finite verbs share guide as their subject.

sections.tip: Identify the grammatical role of each coordinated item, then match that role. A shared to, preposition, or relative pronoun may be omitted without breaking the construction.

sections.heading: Parallelism in comparisons
body: Make comparisons both grammatical and logical. Compare activity with activity, or one object with the corresponding object.
“Reading the novel is more rewarding than watching the film” balances two -ing phrases. Check both sides of than, as, or rather than.

examples.text: Reading the novel is more rewarding than watching the film.
examples.label: Both sides use -ing forms

examples.text: Reading the novel is more rewarding than to watch the film.
examples.label: Infinitive clashes with the -ing form

sections.tip: Compare the grammatical roles and the actual things being compared. Similar first words help, but shared words can be omitted.

sections.heading: Watch the paired connectors
body: Paired connectors include not only…but also, either…or, neither…nor, and both…and. Compare what follows each half.
“Not only for her research but also for her mentoring” balances prepositional phrases. Replacing the second phrase with “she mentored students” breaks that construction.

examples.text: She was praised not only for her research but also for her mentoring.
examples.label: 'for' follows both halves of the pair

examples.text: She was praised not only for her research but also she mentored students.
examples.label: A clause follows 'but also' instead of 'for'

sections.tip: Bracket the full material joined by each connector. Match its grammatical role and preserve the intended meaning.

sections.heading: Keep prepositions consistent
body: A shared preposition can introduce a whole list: “in writing, editing, and publishing.” It can also repeat: “in writing, in editing, and in publishing.”
Keep comparisons in the same form: “interested in cutting costs rather than in reducing service.” Do not change the second part to a different form such as “to reduce service.”

examples.text: She is interested in writing, in editing, and in publishing.
examples.label: 'in' repeats before every -ing form

examples.text: She is interested in writing, editing, and to publish.
examples.label: Last item switches to an infinitive

sections.tip: A preposition may govern coordinated objects without repeating before each. Test the complete construction rather than counting repeated words.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Find a list, comparison, or paired connector. Use the unchanged items to identify the required form.
Choose the matching construction, then reread the complete sentence. A phrase that sounds smooth alone can still fail the surrounding pattern.
sections.tip: Use the unchanged sentence to identify what the coordinated items must do, then insert the choice and check the whole construction. Do not judge only by repeated first words.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: compare logical roles, not repeated words
body: A word may govern a whole coordinated series: to collect, label, and store. Repeating to before each verb is also grammatical. An omitted optional word is not automatically a failure of parallelism.

In complex pairs, bracket the entire structures following not only/but also or either/or. Each must perform the same grammatical job, and a comparison must compare corresponding things rather than an object with an unrelated activity.
How asks about degree; whether asks yes or no. Preserve the intended kind of criterion, not just a similar-looking clause.

examples.text: The protocol requires staff not only to record the temperature but also to explain any sudden change.
examples.label: The paired connectors join two infinitive phrases with the same logical subject.

examples.text: The protocol requires staff not only to record the temperature but also an explanation of any sudden change.
examples.label: The second half is a noun phrase where the first half establishes the staff’s required action.

examples.text: The audit compared how quickly the teams arrived, how reliably their radios worked, and how accurately their logs recorded each response.
examples.label: Each clause asks how well a task was performed; a whether-clause would change the last criterion to yes/no.

sections.tip: Read beyond the first word of each option; shared words are allowed, mismatched grammatical jobs are not.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: The coach told the team to rest well, to eat right, and [[that they stretch daily]].
check.explanation: The first two items in the list are infinitives, 'to rest well' and 'to eat right,' so the third must be the infinitive 'to stretch daily.' 'That they stretch daily' drops a clause into a list of infinitives, 'stretching daily' switches to an -ing form, and 'daily stretching' switches to a noun phrase; each one breaks the pattern the first two items set.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: Painting the fence took longer than [[mowing the lawn]].
check.explanation: 'Painting the fence' is an -ing phrase, so the other side of the 'than' comparison must match: 'mowing the lawn' is correct as written. 'To mow the lawn' pits an infinitive against an -ing form, 'the lawn' compares a chore to a patch of grass, and 'when we mowed the lawn' compares a chore to a point in time.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: The new car is faster, quieter, and [[it uses less fuel]] than the old model.
check.explanation: The list runs on comparative adjectives, 'faster' and 'quieter,' so the third item must be the comparative adjective 'more efficient.' 'It uses less fuel' drops a full clause into the adjective list, 'has better efficiency' switches to a verb phrase, and 'with less fuel use' switches to a prepositional phrase; none of them matches 'faster' and 'quieter.'
